title: Leeds City Council and Xylo: transforming planning with AI
summary: Leeds City Council reports that planning officers using the Xylo Core AI workspace processed over 40% more householder and minor applications each month.
account: Leeds and Xylo developed a workspace that helps planning officers research applications and prepare material for human review. The council's account in the Local Government Association bank states that the pilot launched in mid-October with eight officers, and the council's other records place that launch in 2025. The council’s technical disclosure of 27 November 2025 names the language models and requires officers to review the generated material. On 11 March 2026 Xylo described a separate pilot of its Patch tool with six officers and 33 pre-applications. On 12 March 2026 Xylo cofounder Habs Isabelle Kim reported a 40% increase against a control group. On 23 April 2026 UKAuthority reported that the government's Digital Planning program funded the project and that it was shortlisted for the 2026 Planning Awards. The outlet repeated the council's figure of one day a week saved and added no measurement of its own. In its account of 8 May 2026, the council reports that the pilot had expanded to 20 officers. The council reports that officer interviews and usage data showed over 40% more householder and minor applications processed monthly per officer. It also reports less research work and improved wellbeing among officers. Neither the council nor Xylo provides the throughput denominator, group assignment, baseline totals or analysis needed to assess that comparison. The Patch sample of six officers cannot automatically be treated as the denominator for the Core throughput result. The reported accuracy improvement concerns officers’ judgments of their work. No source reports an independently measured change in decision accuracy. These are original accounts from the council and the supplier, and no independent evaluation of the reported benefit has appeared.
purpose: Help planning officers find and process relevant information while retaining professional judgment.
model_version: The November 27, 2025 council disclosure lists gpt-5-2025-08-07, gemini-2.5-pro, and claude-sonnet-4@20250514. Versions used for individual reported results are unspecified.

ratings.reason: The council reports that each officer processed over 40% more householder and minor applications each month, a measurable gain in service capability.
The council reports that all surveyed officers had improved stress and energy levels and did less research work. No source shows a lasting change.

ai_role.statement: The council describes retrieval of relevant planning material and API calls to language models that generate suggestions and draft text for officer review. Its November 2025 disclosure identifies GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4. The models do not determine planning merits. Reported changes in work and wellbeing come from project-side interviews and usage data. A supplier-reported control group lacks sufficient published methods to establish an independent causal comparison.

fields.summary: Leeds City Council reports that planning officers using the Xylo Core AI workspace processed over 40% more householder and minor applications each month.
fields.account: Leeds and Xylo developed a workspace that helps planning officers research applications and prepare material for human review. The council's account in the Local Government Association bank states that the pilot launched in mid-October with eight officers, and the council's other records place that launch in 2025. The council’s technical disclosure of 27 November 2025 names the language models and requires officers to review the generated material. On 11 March 2026 Xylo described a separate pilot of its Patch tool with six officers and 33 pre-applications. On 12 March 2026 Xylo cofounder Habs Isabelle Kim reported a 40% increase against a control group. On 23 April 2026 UKAuthority reported that the government's Digital Planning program funded the project and that it was shortlisted for the 2026 Planning Awards. The outlet repeated the council's figure of one day a week saved and added no measurement of its own. In its account of 8 May 2026, the council reports that the pilot had expanded to 20 officers. The council reports that officer interviews and usage data showed over 40% more householder and minor applications processed monthly per officer. It also reports less research work and improved wellbeing among officers. Neither the council nor Xylo provides the throughput denominator, group assignment, baseline totals or analysis needed to assess that comparison. The Patch sample of six officers cannot automatically be treated as the denominator for the Core throughput result. The reported accuracy improvement concerns officers’ judgments of their work. No source reports an independently measured change in decision accuracy. These are original accounts from the council and the supplier, and no independent evaluation of the reported benefit has appeared.
